question:
Patient note:
A 65-year-old man with a ten-year history of biopsy-proven micronodular cirrhosis attributed to two decades of heavy beer consumption but abstinent for the past six years walked into the hepatology urgent access clinic this morning at the request of his primary physician, reporting that over the previous month he had to loosen the waist drawstring of his sweatpants by several inches by nightfall, noticed that his shirts draped more tightly across the lower abdomen, and awakened twice during the past week feeling pressure when rolling from side to side; he denied right-upper-quadrant pain, early satiety severe enough to curb caloric intake, shortness of breath, pedal swelling above the ankles, dark or bloody stools, vomiting, hematemesis, lightheadedness, pruritus, progressive fatigue, alterations in sleep–wake pattern, memory lapses, handwriting changes, tremor, or recent falls. He has never bled from varices, never required a paracentesis, and has not been hospitalized during the last two years. The patient’s comorbidities include well-controlled hypertension on losartan 50 mg daily, stage 2 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL, and gout managed with allopurinol 100 mg nightly; he is not taking diuretics, lactulose, rifaximin, non-selective β-blockers, vitamin K, or albumin infusions. Surgical history consists of open appendectomy at age 20 and orthopedic repair of a tibial fracture three years ago. He quit smoking fifteen years earlier after a twenty-pack-year exposure and denies illicit drug use. His father died of myocardial infarction at 71 and his mother has osteoarthritis; no relatives have chronic liver disease. He lives with his spouse, gardens for exercise, follows a modest-sodium diet recommended by a dietitian, and has no known drug allergies. Review of systems is otherwise negative for fever, chills, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, polyuria, or recent antibiotic exposure. On arrival—prior to any venipuncture, intravenous fluids, imaging, or medications—vital signs recorded were temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % while breathing ambient air. The patient sat comfortably on the edge of the examination table, answered questions promptly, named the months of the year backwards without hesitation, recalled three objects at five minutes, and maintained outstretched arms with wrists extended for twenty seconds without a flap; speech was clear, affect neutral, and cranial nerves II–XII intact. Conjunctivae were pink, sclerae showed a subtle lemon-yellow hue, and oral mucosa was moist without fetor. Spider angiomas numbering fewer than a dozen dotted the upper chest, the palms exhibited mild erythema, and no ecchymoses or palmar pallor were observed. Neck veins were estimated at 6 cm H₂O while the patient reclined 30 degrees. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields were clear to auscultation with good air entry. The abdomen protruded hemispherically with the umbilicus flattened but not everted; inspection revealed scant striae and visible bulging of the flanks. Percussion was tympanitic across the epigastrium and supraumbilical region, changing to broad dullness along both flanks that shifted appreciably when the patient rolled onto one side. A fluid impulse was transmitted across the abdominal wall despite the examiner’s ulnar edge applied firmly at the midline, yet the wall remained pliable rather than rock-hard. The liver edge was firm, finely nodular, and palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin on deep inspiration, nontender; the spleen tip was not appreciated. There was trace pitting edema over the dorsum of each foot but none above the malleoli. Muscle bulk appeared preserved in the temporal and deltoid regions. Rectal examination produced heme-negative brown stool. Capillary glucose measured 102 mg/dL. Point-of-care abdominal ultrasonography performed immediately before phlebotomy demonstrated a shrunken heterogeneous liver with irregular capsule, a patent main portal vein with hepatopetal flow of 14 cm/s, a spleen length of 16 cm, and anechoic fluid collecting circumferentially in the peritoneal cavity to a depth of 4–5 cm in Morison’s pouch and the pelvis; hepatic and portal veins were patent and intrahepatic ducts were not dilated. Venous blood drawn minutes later—still before any therapeutic intervention—revealed total bilirubin 2.05 mg/dL, serum albumin 3.82 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 42 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 146 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase 212 U/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 114 × 10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 1.49. Urinalysis from a clean-catch sample showed 1+ bilirubin, moderate urobilinogen, trace protein, and no pyuria. Upright postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any medications displayed elevated hemidiaphragms with compressed lower lung zones but no infiltrate or pleural effusion, and a twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute with a QTc of 421 ms and no acute ischemic changes. Up to this point the patient had received neither diuretics, paracentesis, intravenous albumin, vitamin K, laxatives, nor antibiotics, ensuring that all clinical observations and laboratory values reflect his untreated physiological state at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points each for bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. At presentation:
- Total bilirubin 2.05 mg/dL (2–3) = 2.
- Albumin 3.82 g/dL (>3.5) = 1.
- INR 1.49 (<1.7) = 1.
- Ascites: Bulging flanks, shifting dullness, a fluid wave, and circumferential fluid on ultrasound indicate moderate ascites rather than a trace collection. Moderate-to-severe category = 3.
- Encephalopathy: Attention and recall are intact, with no asterixis or sleep–wake changes. Absent = 1.
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8 (Child-Pugh class B).
Final answer: 8
